reports.name: Junior Caminero
reports.published_report: Forty-six home runs projected at age 23, on a .918 OPS, and the Statcast contact quality almost undersells the power: a .517 xSLG and 93.0 mph average exit velocity put him in rarefied air for a hitter his age. The walk rate at 12.2% is genuinely good, the strikeout rate at 18.3% is fine, and the chase and whiff numbers sit near league average, which means the bat-to-ball profile isn't a liability dragging against the raw damage. The one real blemish is the fielding, where an OAA percentile of 1 suggests he may eventually get pushed off third base entirely. If the glove forces a position change and the defensive value evaporates, you're still left with an offensive force; if he sticks at third, you're looking at one of the game's most complete young hitters.

reports.name: Pete Crow-Armstrong

reports.name: Bobby Witt Jr.

reports.name: James Wood
reports.published_report: The .419 xwOBA tells you everything about the contact quality, 20.8% barrels and 95.1 mph average exit velo leaving almost nothing soft. The 28.6% strikeout rate is the hinge the whole profile turns on: if that number stays that high, the .263 projection carries real drag, and the gap between what he hits and how often he makes contact stays uncomfortable. What saves the argument is the 16.8% walk rate, which is elite and keeps the .387 OBP intact even when the whiff rate bites. At 23, with that raw power and a disciplined enough eye to post a .91 OPS projection across 681 plate appearances, you're not waiting to see if he's good, you're watching whether the strikeouts ever come down enough to let the contact quality fully breathe.

reports.name: Shohei Ohtani
reports.published_report: The xwOBA sits at .413 as a hitter and .257 as a pitcher, and both are in the 94th percentile or better — that's the whole argument in two numbers. His 16.8% barrel rate and 13.9% walk rate tell you the contact quality and the plate discipline are both elite, and the 30.5% whiff rate is the one real tension in the profile: he gives back some of what the .413 xwOBA promises whenever he gets beat by swing-and-miss sequences. On the mound, a 2.71 xERA backed by a 98.1 mph fastball and 30.4% whiff rate against opposing hitters looks like a genuine top-of-rotation arm, not a playing-time curiosity. The projection lines up behind all of it: .291/.395/.557 with 39 home runs across 685 plate appearances, and if the pitching side holds through a full Dodgers season, the conversation about what he is becomes very short.

reports.name: Jacob Misiorowski
reports.published_report: A 40.6% strikeout rate with a 1.91 xERA is not a profile you squint at to find the argument. It announces itself. Misiorowski's 38.3% whiff rate and 2.8% barrel rate explain how a pitcher with a 6.0% walk rate still posts contact numbers this clean: hitters who do make contact aren't hitting it hard, and most of them aren't making contact at all. The projection assumes the walk rate stays in this range, because a command slip that pushes free passes meaningfully higher is the one lever that could complicate an otherwise dominant shape. If the 6.0% holds, 266 strikeouts and a 0.85 WHIP across 180.0 innings is what this looks like.

reports.name: Yordan Alvarez
reports.published_report: The .473 xwOBA sits at the 100th percentile, and there's no meaningful gap between what he does and what the underlying contact quality says he should do. An 18.3% barrel rate paired with a 16.1% walk rate is a profile that doesn't require luck to sustain, because the damage comes from genuine contact quality and a strike zone approach that pitchers can't exploit. The projection's .321/.434/.621 line follows directly from a Statcast card that has no soft underbelly — the one real limitation is 25.0 ft/s sprint speed, which caps his defensive utility and makes him functionally a DH, but that's a role constraint, not a skill one. He's the best hitter in the American League, and the numbers argue he earns that description rather than inherits it.

reports.name: Kevin McGonigle
reports.published_report: The .355 xwOBA tells most of the story here, but the way he gets there is what makes McGonigle unusual: an 18.4% chase rate that sits in the 99th percentile, paired with a 14.4% walk rate, means he's getting on base by genuinely refusing bad pitches rather than by luck on balls in play. The exit velocity profile is soft, 88.0 mph average with a hard-hit rate of 36.4%, so the .432 projected SLG hinges entirely on his ability to punish mistakes when he does swing. If the approach holds at the MLB level, he's a .384 OBP middle-infielder who doesn't need to hit the ball hard to hurt you. If pitchers find a way to neutralize his patience, the power won't cover for it.

reports.name: Kade Anderson
reports.published_report: A 1.20 ERA and 0.70 WHIP across 82.3 innings at AA is the kind of line that makes you check whether the level is right, and the translation says it is. Anderson's 12 walks against 119 strikeouts produce a K-BB% that translates to 21.4% in a league where the average starter sits at 13.5%, and his translated walk rate of 2.1 per nine lands more than a full walk below the MLB mean. The command is the spine of the profile: if it plays up in the majors the way it's played at AA, you're looking at a mid-rotation arm or better; if the stuff gets exposed against better hitters and the walks climb toward league average, you're left with a multi-inning arm who misses enough bats to stick. One to two years out, with this much control at this age, the floor alone is worth something.

The walk rate translates to 13.0% at the MLB level against an average of 8.5%, and that kind of plate discipline tends to survive the trip up. If the power grows into the approach, he's an everyday shortstop; if the bat speed plateaus and the ISO shrinks, the .414 OBP still builds a real career, just not a star one.

Vargas almost never chases, 22.4% puts him well into the top tier of the league, and his 14.4% barrel rate translates that contact quality into real power, which is why the projection lands at 31 home runs despite the batting average drag. The Statcast bat is legitimate; the batting average will stay suppressed until he converts more of that quality contact into hits, and the 14th-percentile OAA says he is carrying defensive baggage that makes a low average harder to absorb. If the hit-tool gap narrows at all, you are looking at a genuine middle-of-the-order bat, and if it does not, .799 OPS at third base for the White Sox is still a real outcome.

reports.name: Jesús Made
reports.published_report: The contact is the whole argument here. At 19, posting a 14% strikeout rate at AA across 435 plate appearances, with a translated MLB-equivalent of 17.6% against a league that strikes out at 22.0%. That's a teenager with legitimate plate-to-bat skills at a level most 22-year-olds are still trying to survive. The power (.181 ISO at AA) translates to .141 in MLB equivalent, which is below the 8.5% walk rate that anchors the rest of the profile, and that's where it hinges: if the gap power doesn't develop, what's left is a slick-contact shortstop who runs (32 stolen bases at AA) and gets on base without doing damage. Either a solid everyday shortstop if the bat grows into average power, or a high-contact, low-damage regular who's genuinely useful but lives at the bottom of a good order.

reports.name: Bo Bichette
reports.published_report: The .694 OPS projection tells the story plainly: this is a shortstop whose bat has slid to replacement-adjacent territory for the position. His xBA sits at .277, which grades out well, but that's the whole trick — he makes a lot of contact on pitches he has no business swinging at, with a 40.5% chase rate that sits near the bottom of the league, and when he does connect, the power just isn't there, a 6.2% barrel rate translating to projected .386 slugging across a full 696 plate appearances. The contact skill is genuine enough to keep him from being a black hole, but a shortstop who walks at 6.0% and doesn't punish mistakes is asking his defense and his BABIP luck to carry a lot of weight. If the chase rate ever tightens, the underlying .277 xBA hints at a more useful hitter underneath; if it doesn't, he profiles as a second-division regular whose counting stats will flatter him more than his slash line deserves.

reports.name: Jac Caglianone
reports.published_report: The raw contact quality is elite and the swing-and-miss is a genuine problem, and that's the whole tension in this profile. A 93.0 mph average exit velocity with a 55.7% hard-hit rate is a special kind of loud contact; the .493 xSLG and 14.0% barrel rate back up the projection's 26 home runs as a reasonable floor rather than a ceiling. But a 37.5% chase rate and 27.1% K% say pitchers have already found the answer, and if the zone control doesn't develop, the .311 OBP will be the ceiling rather than a stepping stone. Either a second-division regular who bludgeons mistakes into extra bases while the strikeouts and defense remain tolerable, or the chase rate compounds and the outfield glove (5th-percentile OAA) turns him into a DH who needs a platoon partner to stay on the field.

reports.name: Wilyer Abreu
reports.published_report: The xSLG sits at .484 and the barrel rate is 12.8%, but his average exit velocity is only 90.0 mph — he's generating elite damage on contact without overwhelming raw force, which is a profile that tends to be kinder to pitchers than it looks on paper. The projection trusts it anyway: 28 home runs across 673 plate appearances with a .782 OPS. What he's not is a batting average asset; the .258 xBA explains why the projection lands at .252, and that gap between his slugging profile and his hit profile is the whole tension here. If the barrels keep coming at this rate, he's a legitimate 28-homer outfielder who makes up for a middling average with enough walks and sneaky speed to be a genuine everyday piece in Boston's lineup.

reports.name: Luis Arraez
reports.published_report: A 4.4% strikeout rate is almost incomprehensible, sitting at the absolute ceiling of the leaderboard, and that's the whole engine here. Arraez doesn't beat you with force: his 87.1 mph average exit velocity and 20.6% hard-hit rate sit at the bottom of the league, yet he projects to a .319/.357/.438 line across 672 plate appearances because he simply refuses to miss the ball. The xBA of .286 reflects elite contact quality on a per-contact basis, even as the xSLG of .377 confirms that when he does lift it, there's not much there. reports.name: Chase DeLauter
reports.published_report: That 20.7% chase rate is the engine of this profile, sitting in the 95th percentile and dragging the whole offensive picture upward. DeLauter makes an unusual amount of contact for how hard he hits — a 91.3 mph average exit velocity paired with a 14.3% strikeout rate is genuinely rare, and the .275 xBA reflects that the contact is landing, not leaking. The barrel rate at 6.5% is the honest limitation, which means the projected .799 OPS is more line-drive power than over-the-fence thunder, and the 17 home runs in the projection are about as good as it gets if the barrel rate doesn't climb. Everything else holds, and you're looking at a legitimate everyday hitter with a plus hit tool; if the barrels stall out and the sprint speed at the 30th percentile limits him positionally, he settles into a useful but less exciting regular.

reports.name: Yoshinobu Yamamoto
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the foundation of everything here. At 5.7%, Yamamoto sits well inside the top tier of the league in limiting free passes, and that command is what makes a 23.8% strikeout rate play bigger than it looks in isolation. He's not racking up punchouts so much as refusing to give hitters anything to work with, holding a .275 xwOBA and a 3.11 xERA through the current MLB sample. The projection calls for a 2.96 ERA over 182.7 innings, and the contact profile backs that number up: 35.1% hard-hit rate and 87.6 mph average exit velo suggest he's keeping the ball off the fat part of the bat consistently enough to sustain it. Health is the only variable left; everything else in this profile reads ace.

reports.name: Daylen Lile
reports.published_report:
The sprint speed is elite. Everything else is the problem.

At 29.3 ft/s, Lile has genuine plus-plus wheels, and the projection credits him for it with 16 projected steals across 652 plate appearances. But the Statcast batting profile is a soft 39th percentile xwOBA sitting on a 37.8% chase rate, and a 5.9% walk rate that turns the speed into decoration rather than a weapon. The barrel rate is fine, the hard-hit rate is not, and a .299 projected OBP tells you what happens when someone with that contact profile also won't take a free pass.

If the chase rate ever comes down, the speed and the decent barrel rate combine into something genuinely useful. If it doesn't, the projection's .713 OPS is probably the ceiling, and he's a bench outfielder whose legs make a roster.

reports.name: Angel Genao
reports.published_report: The contact-and-patience combo is what makes this profile hum. Across AAA & AA in 2026, Genao is hitting .300/.401/.474 through 419 plate appearances, with 60 walks against just 68 strikeouts — a discipline profile that translates to an 11.5 BB% and a K% sitting below league average at the MLB level. The power is the open question: his .174 ISO in the minors translates to .141 at the MLB equivalent, a tick below average, which means if he doesn't add loft or pull-side juice, he becomes a shortstop who gets on base rather than one who damages you. If the hit tool holds and the walks travel, he grows into a low-end everyday regular; if the power translation stays thin, what's left is a bench bat who can still take a walk.

reports.name: Jake Bauers
reports.published_report: The tension in this profile is that the contact quality and the strikeout rate are pointing in completely different directions. A 92.6 mph average exit velocity with a 52.9% hard-hit rate and a 20.4% chase rate is a disciplined, loud-contact hitter; a 25.6% strikeout rate against that kind of contact quality means the swing-and-miss comes from within the zone, not from getting lured out of it. The .368 xwOBA and .482 xSLG say the damage, when it comes, is genuine, and the 13.6% walk rate gets him on base enough that the strikeouts don't hollow out the line entirely. If he stays healthy and gets 532 plate appearances, the projection's .851 OPS is a credible translation of what the Statcast profile already shows — the whole thing hinges on playing time, because the fielding and speed grades say he won't be earning extra roster goodwill with his glove or his legs.

The 99.5 mph fastball is what generates a 37.5% chase rate that ranks among the best in baseball, and when hitters do make contact, the 43.0% hard-hit rate is a real tension point — the stuff misses bats at an elite clip, but the contact allowed carries more juice than you'd want. The walk rate at 9.7% is the lever: if that number creeps up, the hard contact that does land starts to matter a lot more, and a 3.28 xERA becomes something uglier. He's a genuine closer if the command holds, a high-leverage question mark if it doesn't.

reports.name: Kash Mayfield
reports.published_report: The WHIP sitting at 1.2 at A+ is fine, but what makes Mayfield interesting is that the profile underneath it is cleaner than the surface suggests. His K-BB% grades 82nd among pitchers with 20-plus innings in the 2026 combined line, and that's being held down by 22 walks in 53.3 innings at A+, a walk rate that translates to roughly league-average MLB territory and is the one lever he needs to pull. The strikeout stuff translates to just below MLB average at 8.2 K/9, so he's not a profile that can afford loose command — if the walk rate doesn't tighten as he climbs, the ceiling compresses quickly from multi-inning reliever toward organizational depth. Get the walk rate under control and there's a genuine setup-caliber arm here; don't, and you're describing a guy who's always one bad inning from losing a roster spot.

reports.name: Nelson Rada
reports.published_report: The calling card is 31 stolen bases out of 437 AAA plate appearances, backed by a .379 OBP and just 77 strikeouts in those same trips — a profile built entirely on getting on base and going. The power is nearly absent: two home runs and an .08 ISO at AAA translates to .091 in MLB-equivalent terms, well short of the .15 MLB average, which is a meaningful gap and not a quirk of the level. If the speed reads true at the next level and the walk rate holds, his 12% at AAA translates to a tick above-average 10.3% in MLB terms, making Rada a usable table-setter with real on-base skills and a genuine weapon on the bases. If he can't make up ground in raw power, the floor is a bench bat whose value lives entirely in the legs and the .379.

reports.name: Lazaro Montes
reports.published_report: Thirty-two home runs across AAA & AA at 21, with a .314 ISO that translates to .213 against MLB pitching — that's the loud part of this profile, and it's believable across 450 plate appearances. The problem is the strikeout rate: 31% in the minors translates directly to 31% against MLB arms, landing in the 16th percentile of the hitter pool, and a contact floor that makes the .367 OBP fragile the moment the walks dry up. Montes has 65 walks in that sample, so the discipline shows up, and the .561 slugging earns its place, but this entire profile hinges on whether the power is loud enough to carry a strikeout rate that will get exposed against quality spin. If it does, he's a platoon bat with genuine thump; if the swing-and-miss tightens in the bigs and the ISO drops even modestly, the bench is the landing spot.

reports.name: Brandon Pfaadt
reports.published_report: The xERA of 3.82 is the honest number here — contact quality lands right in the middle of the pack, and a 6.6% walk rate is genuinely good. But a 15.6% strikeout rate is a real problem, sitting at the 7th percentile, and a 20.1% whiff rate doesn't give you much confidence that the swing-and-miss will show up when he needs a punch-out. The 2475 rpm fastball spin is the one loud tool, and if that plays into more whiffs at the top of the zone it opens a different ceiling, but right now he's surviving on contact management and command rather than missing bats. Without a strikeout bump, you're looking at a back-of-the-rotation arm who logs innings, posts a serviceable ERA, and doesn't hurt you, which is more or less what the 3.98 projection says.

reports.name: Zach Ehrhard
reports.published_report: The .403 OBP at AAA is the whole argument, and the translation backs it up. Ehrhard's walk rate converts to 12.3% at the MLB level, well clear of the 8.5% MLB average, while his strikeout rate lands almost exactly at league average — a patient hitter rather than a free-swinger who got lucky on balls in play. The ISO translates to .149, sitting right at the MLB mean, so the power isn't the carrying tool here; the approach is, and 16 stolen bases across 457 AAA plate appearances add a wrinkle that fits a center fielder with that kind of on-base floor. If the walk rate holds against better stuff, he's a useful bench bat with real on-base value; if the discipline regresses, a .149 translated ISO doesn't leave much margin.

reports.name: Sean Burke
reports.published_report: The fastball spin is the whole engine here: 2583 rpm ranks at the 96th percentile, and it's what makes a 94.9 mph heater play well above its raw velocity. Burke's 27.4% strikeout rate reflects that, with batters chasing at 32.3% and missing enough to push him into the upper tier of contact suppressors, even if the 25.6% whiff rate sits right at the middle of the league. A 3.58 xERA backs the projected 3.44 ERA, and 179.3 innings suggests a durable mid-rotation workhorse if the profile holds. The dependency is simple: if hitters adjust and the strikeout rate slips toward what the whiff rate suggests as a ceiling, you're left with a back-end arm who competes but doesn't miss bats comfortably enough to anchor a rotation.

reports.published_report: The walk rate tells you everything you need to know about the floor: 3.8% BB% is at the literal top of the scale, and when you pair it with 36.5% strikeouts, you get a reliever who almost never hands the game away before the hitters even swing. The xwOBA of .232 and xERA of 2.21 both land at 99th percentile, meaning the underlying profile isn't chasing the surface ERA, it's confirming it. Hard-hit rate sits at 42.2% and average exit velocity at 90.9 mph, which looks like a contradiction until you see the barrel rate is 3.4% — hitters are making contact but not squaring it up, which is what a 100.4 mph fastball with low spin tends to produce. The projection of 34 saves and a 2.07 ERA over 58.6 innings is the reasonable translation of a profile this clean, assuming health holds.

reports.name: Trea Turner
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile tells a hard story: a .300 xwOBA and a 5.8% walk rate from a 33-year-old shortstop is a bat that has genuinely slipped, not one hiding underlying quality behind bad luck. The contact metrics cluster in the middle of the league, the chase rate sits in the 22nd percentile, and the projection's .712 OPS across 704 PA is the honest output of all of it. What saves the profile as a fantasy asset is the 98th-percentile sprint speed, which translates directly into the 25 projected stolen bases and keeps him relevant in run-scoring contexts even as the stick fades. If the legs hold, he's a counting-stats contributor with a weak average; if they don't, what's left is a below-average bat without the speed tax to offset it.

reports.name: Rafael Devers
reports.published_report: The contact profile is genuinely uncomfortable: a 92.4 mph average exit velocity and 51.0% hard-hit rate sitting next to a 26.4% strikeout rate and a .235 xBA that ranks in the bottom quarter of the league. He hits the ball as hard as almost anyone, and a disturbing share of those balls go nowhere useful, because the 28.8% whiff rate bleeds into weak contact often enough that the batting average never catches up to the raw power. The .449 xSLG and 31 projected home runs follow directly from that exit velocity profile, but the .247/.326 projection is the shape you get when you swing-and-miss at that rate and can't run your way onto base. If the strikeout rate softens even a little, you get a middle-of-the-order bat; if it doesn't, you get a 31-homer DH candidate who bats .247 and costs you an out three times in ten trips.

Tucker's 12.4% walk rate and 24.4% chase rate are where the profile actually lives, both sitting well above a typical big-league hitter, and they explain why a .338 xwOBA comes out of exit-velocity numbers that look completely ordinary. The projection of .247/.345/.401 across 629 PA is essentially the translation of that: a patient, contact-forward hitter who gets on base at a useful clip but no longer profiles as a power threat. What this becomes depends entirely on how much the discipline holds post-injury; if the zone-reading erodes, so does the OBP foundation that makes the whole line workable.

The profile doesn't rely on missing bats at an elite rate, his 27.7% K% and 29.3% whiff rate are good, not dominant, and it runs instead on a 35.9% chase rate that keeps hitters on the defensive and a barrel rate of 5.7% that suggests contact, when it comes, tends to be manageable. The projection of 30 saves and a 2.39 ERA over 70.1 innings in Texas makes sense if the chase rate holds; if hitters learn to lay off the pitch that drives it, the strikeout and whiff numbers don't have enough headroom to compensate on their own.

reports.name: Justin Wrobleski
reports.published_report:
The 3.57 ERA projection sits well ahead of a 4.51 xERA, and that gap is the whole argument about Wrobleski.

His walk rate is elite, 5.1% puts him at the 95th percentile, and that's genuinely load-bearing because a pitcher who doesn't beat himself buys himself margin for everything else. The problem is everything else: a 19.3% strikeout rate in the 28th percentile, a 19.6% whiff rate near the bottom of the league, and a 43.3% hard-hit rate that says hitters are finding the barrel when they do connect. The 2447 rpm fastball spin is a real asset, but spin without swing-and-miss is spin that's being managed, not dominated with. This profile works if the 32.4% chase rate keeps climbing and he converts more of that zone discipline into misses; if it doesn't, the ERA drifts toward the xERA and 154.5 innings of back-end starter production is what you're buying.

reports.name: Christian Scott
reports.published_report: The strikeout rate does the heavy lifting here, and the contact suppression backs it up. Scott's 28.8% K rate grades well above average, and hitters are doing almost no damage on contact, with a 33.9% hard-hit rate and 87.3 mph average exit velocity that both sit comfortably above the league median. The problem is 10.0% walks, because a pitcher who misses bats at that clip but issues free passes at the same rate is always one command stretch from an inning collapsing on him. Tighten the zone and the projection's 3.36 ERA with 139 strikeouts across 118.5 innings starts to look conservative; leave the walks where they are and he's a frustrating mid-rotation starter who teases more than he delivers.

reports.name: Kahlil Watson
reports.published_report: The walk rate is what separates Watson from a typical power-speed prospect buried in the high minors. Across 312 AAA plate appearances this season, he's walking 14% of the time, translating to an 11.2% MLB-equivalent rate while the league average sits at 8.5%, and a .479 slugging with 18 stolen bases fills out a genuinely interesting offensive profile. The problem sitting right next to all of that is 88 strikeouts, a 28% clip that translates to 27.2% at the big-league level, well above average, and that's the hinge: if the plate discipline holds and he doesn't sell out for the power, you've got a useful bench or platoon bat with real on-base ability; if the strikeouts climb and the walks erode, there isn't enough contact to carry him.

reports.name: Druw Jones
reports.published_report: The .367 OBP at AA is the most encouraging thing in this profile, and the most suspicious. A 13% walk rate is genuine discipline, 51 walks in 381 plate appearances at Double-A from a 22-year-old, but that .382 BABIP is doing heavy lifting to get the average to .264, and the underlying pop simply isn't there. Five home runs with a .091 ISO translates to .097 at the MLB level, while the MLB average sits at .150, a gap that turns a passable line into a liability once the BABIP normalizes. The 25 stolen bases are loud, and if the speed and on-base skills survive the translation there's a narrow path to a useful table-setter; if the 29.7% translated strikeout rate holds and the BABIP comes in, what's left is a bench center fielder who runs.

The power translation is the problem: that .150 ISO at A shrinks to .109 against MLB-caliber arms, well short of the .15 MLB average, and if the bat speed or the loft never develops, Ebel's game collapses into a get-on-base-and-run profile without the slugging to force pitchers to negotiate. reports.name: Kyle Stowers
reports.published_report: The hard-contact profile is genuinely elite and genuinely self-defeating at the same time. A 54.5% hard-hit rate sits at the 97th percentile, average exit velocity of 92.1 mph backs it up, and an 11.8% barrel rate gives the power tooth to go with the loud contact. But a 35.4% whiff rate at the 4th percentile means pitchers have figured out how to keep the barrel from the ball often enough that a .228 xBA follows logically from the same swing that generates all that raw force. Across that same sample, the MLB-equivalent K% lands at 28.3%, and the ISO drops from .272 to .158, essentially league-average punch once the level discount is applied. The .368 BABIP is propping up the raw line, and everything hinges on whether Wilder Dalis can tighten the contact profile as competition escalates, because the power and patience aren't yet carrying their own weight at translation. If the strikeout rate compresses and the hit-tool plays up, there's a real hitter here; if it doesn't, the floor is a bench bat propped by athleticism.

reports.name: Hayden Alvarez
reports.published_report: The stolen base number is the loudest thing in this profile: 46 across A+ & A, paired with a .396 OBP that means he's getting on base often enough to use it. The discipline shows in the minors, 63 walks against 90 strikeouts, but the MLB translation is the honest catch — that walk rate sheds to 10.1% while the strikeout rate climbs to 25.1%, and the ISO drops to .121 where the MLB average sits at .150, suggesting the pop that reads as .18 ISO across A+ & A belongs mostly to the level. If the on-base skills translate and the speed stays genuine, he's a usable bench outfielder who earns time through his legs; if the strikeout rate climbs and the ISO doesn't follow him up the ladder, what's left is a speed-only profile without enough bat to hold a roster spot.

reports.name: Spencer Miles
reports.published_report:
The contact suppression is the whole profile. Miles sits in the 96th percentile in both barrel rate and average exit velocity allowed, and those two numbers together explain why a 2.98 xERA coexists with a 18.8% whiff rate that ranks in just the 7th percentile — he's not missing bats, he's ending at-bats with weak contact.

The 6.7% walk rate is clean enough to keep hitters from working around the soft contact, and the projection's 3.17 ERA over 94.1 innings reflects a reliever-heavy workload with 8 holds and zero quality starts, so the role is a high-leverage bridge arm, not a starter despite the SP eligibility.

The dependency is simple: if the contact suppression softens even modestly, there's no swing-and-miss floor underneath it.

reports.name: Brock Wilken
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the only thing keeping this profile above water. Wilken is drawing 67 walks in 390 AAA plate appearances this season, and that discipline translates to a 13.3% walk rate against an MLB average of 8.5%, genuine repeatable skill. The problem is that everything else in the translation is a warning: a .178 average at AAA with a .231 BABIP isn't a luck story, and 113 strikeouts in that same sample translate to 28.2% at the MLB level, well above league average, against power that translates to a .146 ISO right at the average line. The whole profile hinges on whether that walk rate can carry enough OBP to make the strikeouts tolerable at the next level, because the power isn't a differentiator and a first baseman who hits .178 with a .231 BABIP doesn't have a defensive cushion to fall back on. He's dropping nine spots in ValuCast's rankings over three days, and the line explains why: bench depth at best, organizational depth if the contact doesn't improve.

reports.published_report: The walk rate is the one thing working here, and it's working hard. The problem is that the strikeouts don't back it up: 83 punchouts in those same 95.3 innings translate to a 7.2 MLB-equivalent K/9, and a K-BB% that comes out to 11.5% where the league runs 13.5%. reports.name: Trent Grisham
reports.published_report: The plate discipline is genuinely elite — an 18.5% chase rate and 12.7% walk rate that both sit in the upper tier of the league, and the contact quality backs it up with a .338 xwOBA and 90.4 mph average exit velocity. The problem is that none of it converts cleanly into batting average: the .247 xBA sits right around the middle of the pack, and the projection's .215 AVG reflects a hitter whose value lives almost entirely in walks and hard contact rather than hit rate. If the power-to-contact translation holds and he's seeing full-time reps in New York, he profiles as a useful everyday outfielder. If the batting average keeps bleeding, you're looking at a high-OBP, low-floor regular whose value depends entirely on how much lineup context can absorb a .215 hitter.

reports.name: Corey Seager
reports.published_report: The .743 OPS projection over 414 plate appearances is the whole of it: a once-premier shortstop running out of surplus value at the position. A 4th-percentile sprint speed means he's essentially immobile, and if the legs are gone, the defensive profile at shortstop becomes the real risk. The 61st-percentile fielding grade buys him time, but not forever. The 18 projected home runs keep him from being merely a placeholder, and the .325 OBP gives a lineup something to work with, but the .225 average underneath it says the contact quality isn't papering over the athleticism decline. Either a fading starter who gets moved off shortstop mid-contract or a high-priced platoon/DH type, and the legs decide which.

Across AA & A+, Curley has issued just 24 walks in 91.7 innings, a 2.4 BB/9 that translates to 2.9 in MLB context, and the 107 strikeouts over those same innings hint at a guy who can miss bats when he needs to. The translation doesn't flatter him everywhere, though: his K/9 softens to 8.2 in MLB equivalent, just a tick below the majors, and his K-BB% lands at 13.3% where the MLB average sits at 13.5%, leaving almost no margin. If the stuff thins against better contact, the command advantage carrying his profile right now may not be enough on its own. The ceiling is a back-end starter, and if the strikeout rate doesn't hold up a level, you're looking at a reliever who walks almost nobody — useful, not a rotation piece.

reports.name: Jesús Sánchez
reports.published_report: The contact quality is legitimate and the hit tool reads better than his actual numbers — a .274 xBA and .460 xSLG with 46.3% hard-hit rate tell you the bat plays. The problem is the walk rate. At 4.4% BB, he's near the bottom of the league, and a 38.5% chase rate explains why pitchers keep expanding the zone on him. If he can't tighten that discipline, the .313 projected OBP is probably the ceiling, and a .745 OPS outfielder without speed or much defensive value is a roster fringe piece at best. The whole profile hinges on whether the quality of contact can carry him past what his plate approach would normally allow.

reports.name: Levi Wells
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the one thing working in his favor right now. Across 36 innings at AAA, Wells has posted a 2.8 BB/9, and that control profile translates to roughly league-average territory at the MLB level, 3.1 against 3.2, which is genuinely the cleanest part of what is otherwise a thin case. The strikeout rate doesn't carry its weight: 9.0 K/9 at AAA translates to 8.3, a tick below what the league puts up, and a K-BB% of 16% in the minors becomes 13.1% in MLB context, again just shy of average. Eight starts is not enough to trust any of it firmly, and if the command slips even modestly, there's not enough swing-and-miss to compensate. The ceiling here is a depth arm; the floor is a depth arm.

reports.name: Willy Adames
reports.published_report: The .290 xwOBA tells the real story here: this is a shortstop whose contact quality sits well below average, with a 27.9% strikeout rate and a 28.8% whiff rate dragging the whole profile down. The 8.4% barrel rate is fine, roughly league average, which is why 25 home runs are still plausible across 653 projected plate appearances, but the .218 xBA means he's not going to hit his way out of the strikeout hole. What you're left with is a guy who slugs .406 in projection, can play the position, and runs well enough at 27.8 ft/s, but whose .222/.288 projected average/OBP puts him near the bottom of any lineup construction conversation. The OAA sitting at the 1st percentile makes it worse: if the bat-side limitations are baked in and the glove isn't there either, this profile starts to look like a second-division regular at best, and a roster problem at worst.

reports.name: Brandon Nimmo
reports.published_report: The Statcast contact profile is legitimately loud: a .291 xBA and 51.1% hard-hit rate that explain why his xwOBA sits at .371, well above what the projected .269/.340/.439 line reflects. That gap between expected and actual production is the whole tension here, and it resolves one of two ways: either the batted-ball quality starts converting and he hits closer to his ceiling, or the 8.2% walk rate and ordinary barrel numbers keep the OPS around .779 regardless of how hard he hits the ball. At 33, the floor is a useful everyday outfielder; the ceiling, if the contact luck normalizes, is a genuine middle-of-the-order contributor.

reports.name: Conor Essenburg
reports.published_report: The .427 OBP and 56 walks across A+ & A are the loud part of this profile, and they're backed by genuine power: a .267 ISO with 14 home runs in 293 plate appearances puts him in rarefied company at this level. The translation undercuts the whole thing pretty fast, though — that walk rate softens from 19% to 12.3% against MLB arms, and the strikeout rate climbs from 31% to 33.5%, well above a league baseline of 22.0%. If the plate discipline holds shape as he climbs, he becomes a patient corner outfielder with real pop; if the strikeouts keep inflating and the walks compress further, what's left is a bench bat with a pretty BABIP.

reports.name: Bryce Mayer
reports.published_report: The strikeout rate is electric and the ERA flatters him, but the walk rate is the thing to watch. Across 69 innings at AA, Mayer has struck out 100 batters against 34 walks, a 13.0 K/9 that translates to 9.8 at the MLB level, where the average sits at 8.6. The control hasn't caught up: that BB/9 translates to 4.2 while MLB starters average 3.2, and a K-BB% of 24% at the 95th percentile in his pool is doing a lot of work to keep the WHIP at 1.1 despite the free passes. If the walks tighten, there's a legitimate mid-rotation outcome hiding in this profile; if they don't, the ceiling compresses to depth arm, and a K-BB% that good paired with a BB/9 that high is exactly the kind of tension that tends to resolve one way or the other as the competition gets sharper.

reports.name: José A. Ferrer
reports.published_report: The profile is a riddle: 95.7 mph fastball, 6.5% walk rate, and yet hitters make genuine contact when they connect. Ferrer gets the ball in hard enough and keeps it in the zone well enough to post a 3.48 xERA, but his 20.2% whiff rate is a real limitation for a reliever — he isn't missing bats, he's just making hitters hit it softly. The 86.6 mph average exit velocity explains why the results hold up even without swing-and-miss stuff, but a lineup that starts squaring him up more consistently turns a useful middle reliever into a roster question. Project him as a solid middle-innings arm, a 14-hold type who pitches real innings without closing them.

Twenty-three stolen bases at AA in 441 plate appearances, a 12 percent walk rate that translates to 9.9 percent against MLB pitching, and a strikeout rate that would actually beat the majors — those three things paint a real picture of a player who controls the zone and moves. The power is the problem: .093 ISO at AA translates to .095, and the MLB average runs at .150, a gap wide enough that any power development that doesn't come is the whole ceiling argument collapsing. If the bat speed never shows up, what's left is a bench piece who gets on base and runs, which has value, but not everyday value.

reports.published_report: The .244 ISO at A+ is genuinely loud for a 20-year-old shortstop, and it's the whole reason this read exists. Ten home runs across 180 plate appearances with a .506 slugging and 8 stolen bases sketches a toolsy, physical profile that the raw bat speed clearly supports. The translation is honest about the ceiling: that ISO compresses to .157 in an MLB equivalent, barely above the league mean, which is the read right there — the power plays in the aggregate but not at a level that carries a shortstop profile past bench utility. Everything here hinges on whether the hit tool tightens, because 39 strikeouts in 180 PA translates to a 24.4% K rate against the majors, and an OBP that's already ordinary at A+ becomes a liability if contact doesn't improve.

reports.published_report: The power profile at AA is the most interesting thing here, and also the thing that shrinks the most on translation. A .189 ISO across 293 PA at AA reads well on the card, but the MLB-equivalent drops to .146, roughly what a league-average bat produces, and the walk rate translates to 6.6% against a baseline that most big-league regulars clear comfortably. The contact side is quieter than the raw line suggests: a .277 BABIP holding up a .256 average, with 57 strikeouts kept manageable but an OBP of .302 that leaves almost no margin. If the power stays near that translated floor and the walk rate doesn't grow, what's left is a middle-infield profile that fits a bench role more than a lineup spot.

reports.name: Lisbel Diaz
reports.published_report: The power translates. Across A+ & A this season, Lisbel Diaz is slugging .512 with a .231 ISO in 354 plate appearances, and the MLB-equivalent read puts his ISO at .153, right at the .150 MLB average — the thump survives the level jump almost intact. What doesn't survive as cleanly is the patience: 14 walks against 59 strikeouts produces a BB% that translates to 5.1%, well short of the 8.5% MLB average, and a .312 OBP that already leans on his .281 average to stay respectable. The whole profile hinges on whether that contact rate holds as pitchers get more advanced, because if the strikeout rate creeps and the walks don't grow, the power becomes the only tool keeping him on a roster. Either a bench bat with real thunder or organizational depth, and the walk rate is what separates those two outcomes.

reports.name: Jack Cebert
reports.published_report: The walk rate is doing real work here. Across AA & A+, Jack Cebert has issued 25 walks in 82.6 innings, a 2.7 BB/9 that translates to 3.1 at the MLB level, essentially league average, and the K-BB% of 20% sits at the 88th percentile in his pool. The problem is the strikeout side: 96 punchouts across AA & A+ is a 10.5 K/9 in the minors, but the MLB-equivalent translation lands at 8.5, right where the average MLB pitcher lands. That gap between what the walk rate promises and what the strikeout rate actually delivers is the whole tension in this profile. If he holds his command and finds a tick more swing-and-miss against better hitters, there's a backend starter scenario worth tracking; if the K rate settles where the translation suggests, he becomes a depth arm who survives on location until a bad week ends his rotation spot.
